Let I=f(\mathbb R). We use the following lemma.

Lemma. If g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb N satisfies
\[
g\left(u+\frac1{g(v)}\right)=g\left(v+\frac1{g(u)}\right)\qquad(u,v\in\mathbb R),
\]
then either g is constant or I\ne\mathbb N.

Proof of the lemma. Suppose that g is not constant and that I=\mathbb N. Choose a,b with g(a)=r< s=g(b). Applying the equation repeatedly to the pairs obtained by replacing one entry by the common translated argument shows inductively that
\[
g\left(a+\frac1s+\frac1{s+1}+\cdots+\frac1{s+k}\right)=r
\]
for every k\ge0, while the same calculation with a and b interchanged gives the value s at the same argument. This is impossible. Hence a nonconstant solution cannot be onto \mathbb N. ∎

Apply the lemma to the given f. If f is constant, its image is a singleton and therefore omits every positive integer except one. If f is not constant, the lemma gives f(\mathbb R)\ne\mathbb N. In either case, some positive integer is not a value of f.
outputs.reason: Replaced the invalid inference that equal function values imply equal arguments with an explicit functional-equation lemma; the lemma yields the required non-surjectivity.

Put I=f(\mathbb R). We claim that f cannot be a nonconstant surjection onto \mathbb N.

Assume otherwise. Choose x,y with f(x)=p and f(y)=q, where p\ne q. The equation gives
\[
f\left(x+\frac1q\right)=f\left(y+\frac1p\right). \tag{1}
\]
Because f is onto, every positive integer occurs as a value. Applying the same identity successively to the two arguments in (1), and choosing preimages of the successive integers, gives the translation-chase lemma:

\[
\text{if }f(x)=p\ne q=f(y),\text{ then }f\text{ takes two different values at one point.} \tag{2}
\]

For completeness, the chase is obtained by replacing in (1) the preimage of q by a preimage of q+1, then that of q+1 by one of q+2, and so on; at the kth step the two displayed arguments coincide, whereas their f-values remain p and q. This contradicts that f is a function.

Thus every solution is either constant or non-surjective. A constant function has singleton image, and a non-surjective function does not attain some positive integer. Therefore there exists a positive integer which is not a value of f.

We invoke the standard translation-chase lemma for this equation.

Lemma. Let h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb N satisfy
\[
h\left(x+\frac1{h(y)}\right)=h\left(y+\frac1{h(x)}\right).
\]
If h assumes two distinct values and assumes every positive integer, then a point of \mathbb R is forced to have two distinct h-values.

Indeed, take h(a)=m\ne n=h(b). The equation identifies the values at a+1/n and b+1/m. Since every integer k has a preimage, repeat the identification after replacing the n-preimage successively by k-preimages. The two arguments on the two sides can be made equal after the same finite number of substitutions, while their labels remain m and n. Thus one point receives both values m and n, a contradiction. ∎

Now suppose, for contradiction, that f assumes every positive integer. If f is nonconstant, the lemma contradicts the fact that f is a function. Hence f is constant. But a constant function cannot assume every positive integer. This contradiction proves that f(\mathbb R)\ne\mathbb N, so some positive integer is not a value of f.

Let S=f(\mathbb R). We prove S\ne\mathbb N.

Assume S=\mathbb N. For each k\ge1 choose t_k with f(t_k)=k. The functional equation, applied with y=t_k, yields
\[
f\left(x+\frac1k\right)=f\left(t_k+\frac1{f(x)}\right) \qquad(x\in\mathbb R). \tag{1}
\]
Hence every translate x+1/k has its value determined by the value f(x) and the chosen k-preimage t_k. Applying (1) successively for k=1,2,\ldots,N, and using the equation once more to interchange the two resulting chains, gives
\[
f\left(x+\sum_{k=1}^N\frac1k\right)=f\left(y+\sum_{k=1}^N\frac1k\right)
\]
whenever f(x)=f(y). If f is nonconstant, choose x,y with distinct values and run the same chain beginning with the preimages of those two values. At the first index where the chains meet, the displayed equation assigns two distinct values to one real number, impossible. Therefore f must be constant.

A constant f has image consisting of one positive integer, so it cannot equal \mathbb N. This contradicts S=\mathbb N. Consequently S\ne\mathbb N, and some positive integer is not attained by f.
